core.text: Three common verbs make **the future of the irregular verbs (ero = I will be, potero = I will be able, ibo = I will go)** their own way. *Sum* uses a special stem *er-* with the ordinary endings: *erō, eris, erit, erimus, eritis, erunt*. *Possum* is just *pot-* + that: *poterō, poteris, poterit*. *Eō* keeps its stem *ī-* and takes the -b- future: *ībō, ībis, ībit, ībimus, ībitis, ībunt*. Latin name: *futūrum verbōrum anomalōrum*.
The future in English is *will* + verb: *I will be, I will be able, I will go*.
erō / poterō like the present endings of sum on er-; ībō like laudābō. Volō, nōlō, mālō and ferō are regular third-conjugation futures: volet, nōlet, mālet, feret.

invented.la: Crās Rōmam ībimus et amīcōs vidēbimus.
invented.en: Tomorrow we will go to Rome and see our friends.

core.text: *erit* (will be) looks like the ending of **the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense)**: *laudāverit* (will have praised). If *er-* stands alone it is the future of *sum*; if it is glued to a perfect stem (*laudāv-erit*) it is the future perfect.

more.text: From the learner's notes (week 20): compounds of *sum* follow it (*aderō* I will be present, *aberit* he will be away), and compounds of *eō* follow *eō* (*redībit* he will return, *exībit* he will go out).
Watch the two imperfects that rhyme with these futures: *eram* (I was) versus *erō* (I will be); *ībam* (I was going) versus *ībō*. The vowel after the stem decides.

teach.title: What these forms do
teach.say: The same handful of very common verbs make their future their own way: the future of the irregular verbs (erō = I will be, poterō = I will be able, ībō = I will go). They mean what any future (the 'will do' tense) means; most of them simply are not built from a plain stem plus *-b-* or *-ē-*, so they are learned as one small set.

check.ask: Tap the verb that is about tomorrow.

teach.title: sum: the stem er-, and anything fastened in front of it
teach.say: *Sum* builds its future on *er-*, with endings you already know: *-it* for he, she or it, *-unt* for they. Whatever is fastened to the front of it changes nothing else — *aberit* he will be away, *poterit* he will be able, which is simply *pot-* with the plain form behind it. If you can build the plain one you can build all of them. What can be done follows in the infinitive (the 'to' form): *recitāre poterit*, he will be able to recite.

show.say: the stem er- with -it and -unt behind it

check.ask: Write the future of sum for 'he' and for 'they'.

teach.title: sum: the other four persons
teach.say: The rest of the column takes the ordinary endings on that same *er-*: *-ō* for I, *-is* for you, *-imus* for we, *-itis* for you all. The 'I' form ends in *-ō*, as every future does, and not in the *-m* the imperfect used — that single letter is what keeps 'I was' and 'I will be' apart.

check.ask: Write the future of sum for I, for you, for we and for you all.

teach.title: eō takes -b-; volō, nōlō and ferō need nothing new
teach.say: *Eō* makes its future with the *-b-* of the first conjugation: *ībō, ībis, ībit, ībunt*. *Volō*, *nōlō* and *ferō* instead follow the third-conjugation pattern — *-am* for 'I', *-ē-* for the rest, shortened before a final *-t* or *-nt* — giving *volet*, *nōlet* and *feret*. Both patterns are ones you have already met.

check.ask: Write the future of eō for I, for 'he' and for 'they'.

teach.title: Telling erit from erat, and ībit from ībat
teach.say: One vowel separates past from future in the commonest of them: *erat* was, *erit* will be; *poterat* could, *poterit* will be able. The *-a-* looks back and the *-i-* looks forward, and *eō* marks the difference the same way. *Volō*, *nōlō* and *ferō* do not — *volēbat* against *volet* — so read the whole word rather than hunting for one letter.

check.ask: Tap the verb that is about tomorrow, not about the past.

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: These verbs carry most of what a sentence says about later on: where somebody will be, what they will be able to do, where they will go. Here is one already built — *ego crās apud tē erō*, tomorrow I will be at your house. Now set today's fact against tomorrow's and finish the second half yourself.
